articles.title_orig: Three deaths, three states, 24 hours: one day in ICE’s quiet but ‘gruesome’ surge
articles.title_zh: Three deaths, three states, 24 hours: one day in ICE’s quiet but ‘gruesome’ surge
articles.content_orig:
These men in Maine, Georgia and Florida shared no ties – until they became casualties in the latest phase of Trump’s anti-immigration campaign
Gone in 90 seconds: an ‘invisibilized’ ICE is arresting more people than ever
I t was 7am on 13 July this year. A warm, sunny morning, as residents of Biddeford, Maine , left their homes, got into their cars and began their commute. Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero came out of the apartment he lived in with his partner and daughter and drove off in his white car. Minutes later, neighbors heard three pops. Durán Guerrero was dead .
More than 1,200 miles (1,900km) away in Ocilla, Georgia , Jesús Manuel Arenas-Silva was shuffled on to a bus. Private sector guards and Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) officials were beginning the process of transferring him and several other immigrants from one detention center to another nearly two hours away. Ten minutes into the ride, he became unconscious. Doctors at a nearby hospital pronounced him dead .
Less than 24 hours later, Juan Jairo Coronilla Durán, pulled up to a gas station near a busy highway in St Augustine, Florida , as the sun was rising in the bright sky. Soon after, he would lie dead on the road nearby, hit by a semitruck when running away from immigration officers.
There were no ties between Durán Guerrero, Arenas-Silva and Coronilla Durán, but within those 24 hours, the three men suddenly became connected as casualties in the latest phase of Donald Trump ’s aggressive anti-immigration campaign.
Twenty-four hours. Three states. Three people dead. Countless lives changed in seconds.
The men in Maine and Florida were not even ICE’s intended targets for arrest – they became “ collaterals ”, as agency officials call them.
“Three people dying in one day is an amplification of what we’ve already seen,” said Andrew Free, a former immigration attorney and investigative journalist who has for years extensively worked on ICE-related death cases. “The choices that the Trump regime has made since January 2025 have had the consequence of increasing the numbers of people who die in the field and in custody.”
Throughout 2025 and into early 2026, federal immigration officials descended on cities including Los Angeles , Chicago and Minneapolis . They swaggered in militarized gear and brandished their weapons and crowd-control sprays , while engaging in raids and arrests in a high-profile attempt to show that Trump’s promise of “ mass deportations ” would be fulfilled.
An explosion of protests and public backlash grew, reaching a climax after the January 2026 fatal shootings of two US citizens in Minneapolis as they protested against what local leaders called “an invasion” by federal immigration officials .
Since then the flashy immigration enforcement mass operations have all but disappeared . Throughout the rest of 2026, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has switched strategy: more low-key arrest operations by small groups of officers and more 287(g) collaborations with local and state police and sheriffs deputized to make immigration arrests. Also, quicker processing with less representation in immigration courts and White House-directed collaboration to target undocumented children are fueling enforcement that is quieter but just as ruthless.
A summer surge of enforcement means arrests are at a record high, with the majority now being people with no criminal history. And deaths keep ticking up “even though ICE’s current tactics have been less visible than the chaos in Minneapolis at the start of the year”, said Austin Kocher, an assistant research professor at Syracuse University and an immigration data and policy expert, in his Substack posts. At least 31 people have died in 2026 during interactions with immigration officials. Four people have been shot, 25 have died in detention and at least two people, including Coronilla Durán, have died while fleeing officials.
The 24 hours between the mornings of 13 and 14 July stand out as exceptionally deadly.
When contacted for comment, a DHS spokesperson sent along the three previous statements they had issued when the deaths originally happened in Maine, Georgia and Florida .
Much remains unclear about the three deaths in that period, but some crucial details are still known.
On the Monday morning of 13 July when Durán Guerrero left his home in Biddeford, a city in southern Maine, ICE officer David Brouillette and other officers were reportedly looking for a different person , whose last known address was where Durán Guerrero had just exited.
Brouillette, 37, had recently been hired by ICE amid the immigration agency’s push to increase arrests by bringing on more officials. With a blond-brown beard, baseball cap, sunglasses and a green tactical vest marked “POLICE ICE” over a navy T-shirt, Brouillette sat in a federal vehicle and watched the streets.
As Durán Guerrero got into his white car and drove away, Brouillette and the officers spotted him, gave chase and attempted to stop the car.
The next few moments are still unclear, but neighbors suddenly heard the “pops” of gunfire in the quiet neighborhood. Brouillette had fatally shot Durán Guerrero.
A statement from the DHS at the time said that the ICE officers attempted to stop the vehicle, but that Durán Guerrero “attempted to flee”. The DHS added the official fired at Durán Guerrero “ fearing for public safety”.
It has not been verified whether Durán Guerrero drove his vehicle in the way that the DHS stated.
Surveillance footage obtained by the Associated Press appears to show a white car slowly driving in circles at an intersection. The footage was recorded after the shooting, with Durán Guerrero either dead or dying at the wheel.
The video then shows one of ICE’s vehicles ramming into the white car to stop it. Two officers open the driver’s door and Durán Guerrero’s body slumps on to the asphalt. Two more ICE officers rush over.
“He had blood on his head, blood on his face. It was gruesome, just gruesome,” a neighbor told Maine Public Radio. “I believe it was [Durán Guerrero’s] wife that was sitting on the curb across the street, just crying hysterically.”
The Colombian man was 25, with a dazzling smile that lit up his face below closely cropped dark hair. He lived with his partner, Karolina Rojas, and their three-year-old daughter, and he had authorization to live and work in the US. He was a food delivery driver and is remembered by his neighbors as a good man and hard worker.
“My son was a person who left his country to make a future for his family,” Omar Durán, Durán Guerrero’s father, told BluRadio , a Colombian news outlet.
Brouillette, the ICE officer, was hired by the agency after years of employment instability, according to reporting from the Associated Press , the Portland Press Herald and other outlets . He was recruited even though family members have made allegations of a history of violent behavior, including accusations of domestic violence and threats.
Attempts to reach Brouillette for comment were not successful.
About ICE’s recruitment policies, the DHS said: “The ICE Office of Professional Responsibility diligently applies the proper personnel vetting regulations, including guidelines for national security, and evaluates all available information for every applicant based on these factors.” The ICE office of professional responsibility internally investigates any alleged misconduct.
The DHS has still not publicly confirmed Brouillette’s identity as the official who shot Durán Guerrero, nor commented on his alleged personal history. The agency has criticized the media for publishing his name, saying it put officers and their families in danger.
Meanwhile, in Georgia , just after 7am on 13 July, Arenas-Silva sat in an ICE transport bus, surrounded by other ICE detainees.

articles.title_orig: Could Trump revoke Ilhan Omar's citizenship for alleged brother marriage? Ex federal prosecutor breaks it down
articles.title_zh: Could Trump revoke Ilhan Omar's citizenship for alleged brother marriage? Ex federal prosecutor breaks it down
articles.content_orig:
Immigration attorney Michael Wildes explains the evidence required to establish marriage fraud and whether Omar’s claim that DHS has not contacted her impacts the legitimacy of the investigation.
The Trump administration's recent effort to bring the law down on Rep. Ilhan Omar could go as far as seeking to strip the Minnesota congresswoman of her citizenship for alleged immigration fraud. But a criminal investigation is unlikely to yield the results the president wants, according to a former federal prosecutor.
Michael Wildes, an immigration attorney, told Fox News Digital that investigators face a "very high bar" to build a case against Omar after White House border czar Tom Homan confirmed the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is conducting a "criminal" investigation against the progressive "Squad" member.
It all stems from claims that Omar married her brother to gain U.S. citizenship, which she has repeatedly denied.
President Donald Trump has a longstanding feud with Omar going back to when she was first elected in the middle of his first term, and quickly became one of his most vocal critics in Congress. Trump has repeatedly called for Omar to be sent back to Somalia because of her alleged fraudulent activity.
The Trump administration continues to ramp up efforts to denaturalize and deport individuals accused of immigration fraud. And Vice President JD Vance claimed earlier this year that the Department of Justice is investigating Omar for alleged fraud and immigration violations.
But questions remain over what a potential prosecution and denaturalization case against the Somali-born lawmaker would require.
Wildes said that investigators would need to prove beyond reasonable doubt that Omar knowingly entered her marriage — to a man critics allege is her brother — for the sole purpose of evading U.S. immigration laws.
DOJ MOVES TO STRIP CITIZENSHIP FROM 17 PEOPLE ACCUSED OF HIDING DISTURBING CRIMES
U.S. Representative Ilhan Omar speaks during Day 2 of the Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor (DFL) Party Convention in the Mayo Civic Center in Rochester, Minn., on Saturday, May 30, 2026. (Alex Kormann/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images)
"In order to establish a successful marriage fraud case, the government would have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt… that the defendant knowingly entered into a marriage with the primary purpose to evade immigration laws and get a benefit," Wildes said.
Wildes noted that even if Omar and her husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, decided after getting married that their partnership could be a scheme for Elmi to fast pass America’s immigration process, this would not be considered marriage fraud in court.
He continued, "Those are very high bars and thresholds that they would have to surmount. The immigration benefit cannot be a byproduct or secondary consideration. This is not deemed to be illegal."
If evidence was presented to prove Omar and Elmi committed marriage fraud , the Minnesota Democrat could face up to five years in jail, a maximum fine of $250,000, or both.
Wildes also pointed out that there are statutes of limitations that could hinder a potential prosecution and make it more difficult to prosecute Omar for marriage fraud, as that marriage was in 2009. But there is still a pathway for Omar to be denaturalized, which Homan described as a "very serious process" while discussing the investigation into the congresswoman.
"The question is: Do they have it factually, and is it the right thing to do?" Wildes said.
"The question is whether or not inadvertences were made not purposefully and whether or not it's over the top to then denaturalize somebody," he said. "We're talking about taking away a benefit and then banishing them from the United States."
FORMER USCIS OFFICIAL, ACCOMPLICE CHARGED IN ALLEGED $960K CITIZENSHIP BRIBERY SCHEME
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is denying that she has been made aware of any criminal investigation into her after White House border czar Tom Homan confirmed Sunday that the Department of Homeland Security is investigating her. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
For Omar to be denaturalized, the process would have to be related to allegations that she falsified information when obtaining her own citizenship in 2000. Omar claims she was granted automatic citizenship because she was a minor when her father was naturalized.
Congressional records state Omar became a citizen at age 17, but speculation that she was older at the time of her naturalization began after former Minnesota congressional candidate AJ Kern accused Omar’s birth year of being revised on the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library website.
This caused allegations to circulate on social media that she was not a minor at the time, which, if ever proven true, could lead to her denaturalization. Even if her father lied in his citizenship paperwork, this could also potentially lead to Omar being stripped of her citizenship.
Wildes also explained that the government makes a "case-by-case" decision when it comes to pursuing denaturalization cases. He also pointed out the relevancy of an intentional lie as opposed to a mistake.
"If the government were to prosecute for document fraud, we would also want to know whether or not she was represented by counsel, and if there were simple mistakes on her application or inadvertences that may be deemed to be fraudulent," Wildes said.
"Whether or not [these] things are truthful, hypothesized, or can be backed up in fact, will play heavily in that prosecution."
Homan didn't answer whether the federal government has evidence that Omar committed either marriage or immigration fraud , while also declining to go into detail about what particularly DHS is investigating Omar for.
Omar told Fox News Digital just last week that she has not been contacted by DHS or made aware of any ongoing investigation into her marriage or immigration status, saying she isn’t worried about it because "the right wing always had this s--- going."
'SQUAD' DEM DISMISSES FRAUD PROBE SPECULATION AFTER $29M NET-WORTH DROP
But Wildes said her being unaware that she is being investigated is not unusual and doesn’t invalidate Homan’s confirmation of a "criminal" investigation against her.
"The congresswoman's not being aware doesn't change anything," Wildes said. "There is no obligation for the government to show their hand, and they're going to want to make sure that they have a good prosecution, and they don't give anything up in the interim because of the politics that this presents as well."
"I haven't seen anything that I think is worthy of a prosecution," Wildes said. "This is a member of Congress. It may not be your politics, but we have to also make sure that we engage in prosecutions properly and not frivolously."

articles.title_orig: ‘On a scale of 1 to 10, 10’: Trump’s midterm travel schedule underscores GOP troubles
articles.title_zh: ‘On a scale of 1 to 10, 10’: Trump’s midterm travel schedule underscores GOP troubles
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump’s unusual decision to hold a midterm rally in a rural part of Oklahoma, a state long considered a Republican stronghold, signals GOP panic that voters may sit out the election as the president’s popularity wanes.
Political scientists said Thursday’s campaign rally in Durant , a city of about 21,500 people located about 2.5 hours southeast of Oklahoma City, also underscores GOP concerns that a Trump endorsement has decreased in value.
Trump’s first official appearance in the state in six years also comes as a state party leader said Democrats nationally are putting resources into flipping an Oklahoma City-area congressional seat that has been held by Republican incumbent U.S. Rep. Stephanie Bice since 2021.
“I think it’s a signal of how bad things have gotten for the Republicans under Trump,” said Seth McKee, a political science professor at Oklahoma State University.
While Trump won all 77 of the state’s counties two years ago, his approval ratings have dropped across the country , including in Oklahoma, as war with Iran continues and everyday costs continue to rise.
McKee said Trump has become “toxic” to Republicans seeking office and he might cause more harm in places that have highly competitive races.
“He doesn’t hurt in Durant, Oklahoma, but he might be a net negative if he went down to Dallas and campaigned for Ken Paxton,” he said. “… So that’s what we’re dealing with here, which is a real problem. I mean, he’s so unpopular that if you put him in any context where a race is super close, he’s not going to help it, he’s going to hurt it.”
Paxton, a Republican endorsed by Trump, is running in a tight race against Democrat James Talarico for the U.S. Senate seat in Texas. Paxton defeated incumbent U.S. Sen. John Cornyn in the primary runoff.
Trump will campaign in Durant with Republican gubernatorial candidate Mike Mazzei, who the president has also endorsed, the Republican National Committee said. He’s also attending a a separate rally Friday in Mobile, Alabama.
A Republican strategist familiar with midterm planning said Trump is holding his rally in Durant because it is near the Texas border and the Dallas-Fort Worth media market.
A visit there allows Trump to boost Texas candidates and Mazzei at the same time, the strategist said.
But Allyson Shortle, a professor of political science at University of Oklahoma, said there is likely concern that Trump’s endorsement doesn’t carry the weight it once did. Trump’s visit is meant to boost voter participation within the party base.
Even with the president’s endorsement, Mazzei won the Republican nomination by a little over 2,000 votes . He’s set to face Democrat Cyndi Munson in November.
“I think it sort of shows that (Trump) is doing damage control on his base,” Shortle said. “He’s going to the deepest red portions to make sure that they are still on his side and that they will in fact come out for the election. He wants that turnout because elections are won due to mobilization.”
Shortle said the fight for Oklahoma’s Congressional District 5 seat, which encompasses six counties in central Oklahoma, is also garnering unexpected national attention.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has invested resources in Democrat Jena Nelson’s campaign in an attempt to unseat Bice, said Erin Brewer, chair of the Oklahoma Democratic Party.
It’s an unusual move because it’s usually considered a “foregone conclusion” that Oklahoma’s congressional seats will go to Republican candidates, Shortle said.
“If you look at that district in particular, there are a lot of Democratic voters, so they must believe that there is a chance that they could mobilize the Democratic base there to at least have a fighting shot,” Shortle said.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee did not immediately respond to requests by publication.
Brewer said the national involvement from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is a big deal because the race between Nelson and Bice is “so close.”
A recent poll of 500 voters conducted by GBAO Strategies found that Nelson is trailing Bice by only five percentage points. The Washington D.C.-based organization works largely with Democratic campaigns.
“I think what people are seeing is (in) what have been ‘Republican strongholds,’ people are waking up to the way Republican policies really failed them,” Brewer said. “And so I think there’s some bellwether states here that maybe have been ignored for the last few years that they’re going to have to start paying attention.”
Trump’s visit to Durant also shows the “weakness” and unpopularity of Mazzei as a candidate, she said.
“If Trump feels he needs to come and stump for a Republican governor’s candidate in Oklahoma, that should tell you the mood of voters in Oklahoma and that things are shifting,” Brewer said.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi insisted late Monday that Tehran has made no changes to its proposal for a seven-day ceasefire and the phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran awaits a formal U.S. response to the plan via mediators.
Tehran presented the proposal last week, demanding that in exchange for the strait being reopened, the U.S. meets conditions set out in the memorandum of understanding signed in June by Mr. Trump and his Iranian counterpart.
"Our plan, which became known as the seven-point plan, was conveyed to the Americans through the Qatari intermediary," Araghchi told reporters in New York, where he has been for the U.N. General Assembly. "Despite the things that the American president and others said, I said that we are waiting for an official response from America through the intermediary."
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Tuesday that it is developing new weapons to defend the Islamic Republic.
"We are constantly designing and upgrading new and existing weapons to defend ourselves," IRGC spokesman Brig. Gen. Hossein Mohbbi said, without offering any real detail.
"We use all the technologies of the world to build new weapons in order to defend our people and our country, and if necessary, we will use these weapons to defend our country," he said.
Mohbbi said the U.S. had failed to achieve its objectives through military and economic pressure, and predicted that "ultimately, America will be forced to leave the region."
Iran's chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Tuesday that if his country's security was not guaranteed, no infrastructure in the region would be safe from attack, state media reported.
"In a region where we cannot sell oil, no one else will sell oil either; or if our security is not guaranteed, no infrastructure will remain safe," said Ghalibaf, who is also Iran's parliament speaker, according to video released by state TV.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he expected a formal answer on Tuesday from the United States to Tehran's proposal to open the Strait of Hormuz, state media reported.
Qatari intermediaries "presented ideas, and we discussed them; they are set to raise the matter with the American side once more, after which the final U.S. response will be conveyed to us", Araghchi said late Monday.
Iran's top diplomat, who is in New York for the U.N. General Assembly, said "the Qataris hope this will be done by tomorrow".
President Trump denied that he has offered to relieve Iran of some sanctions and unfreeze its funds, writing on Truth Social : "I offered them NOTHING!"
The president was reacting to an Axios story that said Mr. Trump is open to granting sanctions relief in exchange for progress on Iran's nuclear program.
A U.S. official also told CBS News on Monday that Mr. Trump is willing to grant Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds if progress is made on the nuclear issue.
President Trump confirmed to reporters that American and Iranian negotiators exchanged messages through mediators on Monday.
He did not share any details on the talks, saying, "We're going to win."
CBS News reported earlier Monday that indirect U.S.-Iran talks began in the morning. A U.S. official said Mr. Trump is willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds if there is concrete progress on Iran's nuclear program, but there will not be a deal unless the nuclear issues are addressed, and the two sides remain apart on the timing of commitments.
An Iranian diplomatic source told CBS News the primary issue is that the U.S. president does not seem to have a clear position on what he wants from negotiations, making it difficult to move from discussions to a concrete agreement.
Yields in the U.S. bond market cranked higher Monday and again reached their highest levels in roughly two decades, which knocked U.S. stocks further from their record high.
Monday's rise in yields followed the latest swings for oil prices , which have been yo-yoing on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow tankers to flow freely again through the Strait of Hormuz and deliver oil from the Middle East to customers worldwide.
The latest turns came after President Trump said over the weekend he's rejecting an offer from Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear program.
A move by the U.S. to temporarily halt diesel exports amid record-high prices would initially lower costs, but a prolonged ban could drive up domestic gasoline prices, according to Goldman Sachs.
President Trump on Sunday told reporters his administration is "very seriously" considering a ban on diesel exports. Calls to restrict exports of U.S.-refined diesel have picked up in recent weeks, mostly from Republican lawmakers, as a lever they believe will help lower prices. Diesel hit a record $6.53 a gallon on Sept. 22, and has only eased slightly since then, slipping to $6.45 a gallon on Monday, according to AAA data.
The war with Iran is pushing up oil and gas prices , creating widespread financial strain on U.S. motorists , food delivery drivers and farmers .
Yemen's defense ministry said it carried out 356 strikes against Houthi military targets over the past 24 hours, killing or wounding an estimated 476 fighters.
Video posted by the Yemeni military showed strikes on various Houthi positions across several front lines.
Military spokesman Col. Majed al-Nazili said the strikes targeted Houthi command centers, weapons depots, artillery positions, vehicles and other military equipment.
The U.S. and Iran are continuing to have discussions, viewed as positive and constructive, through mediators, but there will not be a deal unless the nuclear issues are addressed, according to a U.S. official.
President Trump is willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds if there is concrete progress on nuclear issues, the official said. Iran has indicated it is flexible on nuclear issues, but the two sides still remain apart on the timing of commitments and who takes which steps first.
The official said the U.S. is skeptical of Iran's promises after it broke the memorandum of understanding by firing on commercial vessels, and is looking for assurances that Iran is serious.
Flying out of Iran has long required patience in the face of restrictions and delays, but new U.S. sanctions have grounded flights on short notice and left war-weary travelers feeling trapped as they try to leave the country.
Passengers who booked tickets out of Iran to Middle Eastern destinations like the United Arab Emirates, Iraq, Oman and Turkey have faced short-notice cancellations as the latest sanctions bite.
Among those scrambling for a way out is Mitra, a 49-year-old woman who had planned to travel to Paris via Istanbul along with her brother, but who now faces a long journey by road to get to Turkey.
"Some airlines are still selling tickets, but they keep getting canceled. It honestly makes us feel completely trapped," she told an AFP journalist in Paris, using a pseudonym for fear of retribution by authorities.
"When we were told that flights had been suspended, we decided to travel to Istanbul by land instead," she said.

In Van in Turkey, they will stay at a hotel, because the wait at the border can be long and chaotic.
"At this point, we're just hoping that we can actually get out. They might even close the land border," she fears.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's $150B buyback could fuel next stock rally
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's $150B buyback could fuel next stock rally
articles.content_orig:
When Nvidia announced a record stock buyback on Monday, the chipmaker's share price was, by one key metric, at its cheapest level in a decade. CEO Jensen Huang saw it as a bargain.
Nvidia's price-to-earnings ratio for fiscal 2028, which begins this coming February, sits at just 14.5, below all of its megacap peers other than Micron . Its average current P/E ratio over the past five years is 62.9, more than double where it is today.
The constricted multiples for the world's most valuable company, now valued at over $5.5 trillion, reflect the sustained historic rate of profitability growth for the chipmaker powering the artificial intelligence boom. The stock is up 23% this year, topping the Nasdaq, but it's not keeping up with expected earnings growth.
Analysts on average expect Nvidia to hit net income of close to $385 billion in fiscal 2028, up 60% from the prior year and more than fivefold over a three-year stretch.
So on Monday, Nvidia said it's authorized an additional $150 billion to its share buyback program. That's on top of an $80 billion repurchase plan announced in May, when the company also boosted its quarterly cash dividend to 25 cents per share from 1 cent.
The latest buyback is a "clear-cut message" that management thinks its stock is undervalued, said Karan Ramchandani, managing director at Post Oak Group, in an interview. "If you look at the P/E ratio, the earnings are are scaling up faster than the share price," Ramchandani said. "It's a very healthy mark of a company looking at their own stock buybacks as the best investment they could do in the coming year."
The stock rose almost 2% on Monday, when the company also announced new software and hardware solutions to control AI agents.
Nvidia is stepping up its capital return plans as its revenue and cash flow explode because of demand for the company's graphics processing units used to build and run AI models and services.
The company has signaled continued growth through early 2028, telling investors in August that it sees 70% sales growth in its fiscal 2028, which implied the company will do hundreds of billions more in sales than Wall Street had previously forecast.
Huang told investors at a Goldman Sachs conference earlier this month that Nvidia was "misunderstood" and implied that it should be more highly valued both for its growth as well as its value measured by future earnings.
"We are the world's first and only growth value stock," Huang said. "People are trying to figure out which one we are. We are both."
Huang is putting his company's money where his mouth is after telling CNBC's Jim Cramer last month that, "Buying back Nvidia stock is a tremendous opportunity."
Nvidia previously said it planned to return about half of its free cash flow to investors through share repurchases and buybacks. Its share count could drop by 4% if the chipmaker spends its entire current authorization.
"We're going to generate a lot of cash in the coming years," Huang said on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Monday. "As we generate more cash, we'd like to be able to return it back to shareholders."
Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, told CNBC's "Fast Money" on Monday that investors appear worried that growth rates will slow after a monstrous few years.
"It's just really hard for investors to get comfortable that that's going to continue," Munster said. "That downward slope of growth rate, that's the reason why it trades at that compressed multiple."
Nvidia's fiscal 2028 P/E ratio puts it behind behind Apple (35.5), Alphabet (22.6), Microsoft (21.7) and Amazon (23.2) as measured for a similar period. It's also less highly valued than its primary AI data center chip rivals including Broadcom (18.2), Advanced Micro Devices (38.2) and Intel (54.7). None of Nvidia's rivals are forecasting 70% sales growth next year.
Broadcom's silicon business is built around developing custom chips with companies such as OpenAI and Google. AMD competes with Nvidia in GPUs, but with a small fraction of the market share. Intel makes central processors and has dabbled in AI chips, but doesn't have a competitive product to Nvidia's GPUs.
Ben Reitzes, an analyst at Melius Research, has a buy recommendation on the stock and said it "deserves to be higher given its growth rate."
"Buying back stock in a bigger and bigger way is going to really help it solve that problem and get a better valuation," Reitzes told CNBC's "Closing Bell" on Monday.
UBS analysts said in a note on Monday that Nvidia's stepped-up share repurchases could add 8 cents per share to the company's calendar year 2027 earnings, which it estimates at $17.16.

articles.title_zh: Senate GOP to press Jack Smith on Trump Jan. 6 probe as DOJ targets investigators
articles.content_orig:
Morning Rundown: Attorney blasts Cornell over rape allegations, Jack Smith faces Senate GOP on Jan. 6 probe, and why Week 3 was one of the wildest in NFL history
WASHINGTON — Former special counsel Jack Smith, who brought two since-dismissed federal criminal cases against Donald Trump, is expected to face questions on Tuesday from the president’s allies in the Senate about his handling of his investigation into Trump’s efforts to overturn his 2020 election loss in the lead-up to the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol .
Smith is set to testify before the Senate Judiciary Committee amid the Justice Department’s push to target law enforcement officials involved with Smith’s investigation into Trump’s attempts to overturn the 2020 election results as well as the probe into his handling of classified documents after he left office in January 2021.
Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, has repeatedly criticized Smith. The title of Tuesday’s hearing, which Grassley will chair — “Oversight of Jack Smith’s Abuse of Authority and the Targeting of Republicans and Related Matters” — suggests a potentially combative hearing. With it, Grassley asserts that Smith misused his investigative powers and politically targeted Republicans. Smith, who as a career prosecutor went after Republicans and Democrats, has denied such allegations.
Grassley said in a statement ahead of the hearing that Smith “must answer” for what the senator portrays as “rampant abuse of authority and political targeting” funded by American taxpayers.
“If Jack Smith did that to Democrats, you’d never hear the end of it,” Grassley said in the statement, adding that his goal is holding accountable the Justice Department for actions taken during the Biden administration.
Smith did not issue a statement in advance of his testimony.
Smith has said he believes a jury would have convicted Trump in the 2020 election-related case had it gone to trial and that the notion that his decisions were “ influenced or directed by the Biden administration or other political actors is, in a word, laughable .” Smith’s final report in the election interference case stated that Trump “ inspired his supporters to commit acts of physical violence ” at the Capitol on Jan. 6.
Trump pleaded not guilty in Smith’s Jan. 6 case and denied after the attack that he incited his supporters, calling his remarks at a rally that day “totally appropriate.” Trump later described Jan. 6 defendants as “hostages” and gave them mass clemency upon his return to office.
The Trump administration last year launched a so-called grand conspiracy investigation looking at actions taken by federal law enforcement officials dating back to 2016, which would fall outside the typical five-year statute of limitations for most federal crimes .
The Trump administration also has purged FBI and Justice Department officials involved in past Trump investigations. Defense attorneys for current and former officials informed a court last week that DOJ officials appear interested in probing the circumstances of an August 2022 FBI search of Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, during which agents found classified documents that were at the heart of one of the since-dismissed Trump cases.
Joe diGenova, who was a federal prosecutor during Ronald Reagan’s presidency, headed up the “grand conspiracy” investigation until he left the Justice Department this month. He told NBC News that “ lanes got crossed ” in his final days.
In his first public testimony before Congress earlier this year, Smith told the House Judiciary Committee that he would not be intimidated and predicted that the Trump administration would attempt to launch a criminal case against him. Months later, one of Trump’s allies on Capitol Hill, Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, asked the Trump administration to investigate Jordan’s assertion that Smith “seemingly” made false statements in congressional testimony.
Smith’s lawyers said he provided “truthful, responsive answers” and that Jordan’s referral “reflects a chilling eagerness to weaponize the justice system by attacking a career, nonpartisan public servant who faithfully and fearlessly performed his duties by following the facts and the law.” Former federal prosecutors have told NBC News that the Justice Department would have a tough time bringing a perjury case against Smith.
Smith is not expected to discuss the classified documents investigation because Trump-appointed U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon ordered that that portion of his report as special counsel cannot be released. The Justice Department has taken the position that answering questions about that investigation would violate Cannon’s order.
Ryan J. Reilly is a justice reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: As the U.S. signals a smaller Middle East footprint, Turkey is ready to step in
articles.title_zh: As the U.S. signals a smaller Middle East footprint, Turkey is ready to step in
articles.content_orig:
Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at United Nations headquarters in New York, Sept. 22. Seth Wenig/AP hide caption
ISTANBUL — It was a milestone moment. Leaders from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan were meeting at a palace overlooking the Grand Mosque in Islam's holy city of Mecca.
Sitting side by side that day, on Aug. 7, at hardwood desks set against a backdrop of silk drapery, the three leaders put pen to paper and signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement.
Described by some as the birth of a "Sunni Security Triad," the agreement combines Saudi Arabia's oil wealth, the growing defense might of Turkey, which already fields NATO's second largest military, and Pakistan's nuclear capabilities. It includes NATO's Article 5-style language, that any armed attack on one of the three Sunni Muslim states is regarded as an attack on all of them, and a commitment between them to exchange intelligence and defense technology.
But perhaps more important than the contents of the deal, the agreement symbolizes a cornerstone of an emerging regional security architecture and a hedge against post-U.S. geopolitical uncertainty.
According to Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Ankara was a main driver of the talks that went on for three years. And analysts say it was pushed by Ankara's vision that aims to slowly establish Turkey as a central player in the Middle East, a region rocked by years of war that has shaken longstanding power dynamics.
Turkey's broadening defense-industrial base leaves the country less dependent on the West militarily (though it still craves F-35 jets from Washington). It has also widened its military reach: it has bases in Somalia, Qatar, Libya and is playing an increasingly central role in shaping Syria as it emerges from a decade of civil war. Turkey has also deftly used cultural soft power — its TV shows are watched across the region — and humanitarian causes — building schools across the region — to gain influence. And Turkey has cast itself as a capable mediator to help bring an end to global conflicts, from Ukraine to Iran.
Turkey's bid for greater regional influence comes at a time when the region has been hit by profound shocks that started with the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, and continues with the stalemated, seven-month-old U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. Those have seen Iran defiant but diminished, with its network of proxies across Syria and Lebanon in ruins. There's growing talk in Washington of the U.S. reducing its Middle East security footprint in the aftermath of the war, amid persistent questions from the region about the value of the U.S.'s security umbrella.
From left: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif sign a trilateral defense agreement in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, on Aug. 7. Turkish Presidency/Murat Cetinmuhurdar/Handout/Anadolu via Getty Images hide caption
Turkey's ambitions to fill any void though face some real obstacles. Years of economic mismanagement have led to persistent high inflation, a weak currency and rising energy import costs, straining state resources. Its biggest challenge though might come in the form of an increasingly assertive and aggressive Israel.
"Turkey's regional ambitions clearly exceed its current economic means. That doesn't make Turkey a militarily or strategically weak country," says Asli Aydintasbas, director of The Turkey Project at the Brookings Institution. "But Ankara understands that it's been unable to translate its growing influence into a Turkish-led order beyond its immediate periphery."
The Ottoman Empire controlled and ran much of the region from Istanbul for nearly half a millenium before it collapsed in the aftermath of World War I. Many in the Turkish government led by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan see its regional role in civilizational terms and believe that the Ottoman Empire essentially offered a better model of governance and cohesion than the nation-states that replaced it.
" I think that there is a sense of a manifest destiny among Turkey's current ruling elite that Turkey's destined to be the region's heavyweight," says Aydintasbas. But Turkish foreign policy is far more restrained and realistic, tempered in part by its own economic struggles. Aydintasbas says Ankara is trying to manage regional disorder to protect its vital national interests rather than dominate or build a neo-Ottoman empire.
Turkey, says Aydintasbas, understands the region is likely entering a post-U.S. phase after the war with Iran, and it's playing the long game.
"Without a clear U.S. win, gradually, U.S. influence in the region will decline and Turkey will be there to step in," says Aydintasbas.
President Trump has long questioned the value of U.S. bases in the region and has overseen a drawdown of U.S. troops in Syria and Iraq. The U.S. also seems to have blessed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement.
Aydintasbas says the region is now craving stability over values-based democratic transition because there has been too much suffering.
Syria has emerged as the central laboratory for Turkey's growing influence. Following the collapse of Bashar al-Assad's regime in 2024, Ankara achieved major core objectives: It secured multibillion-dollar contracts for postwar Syrian reconstruction and became Syria's main partner helping it rebuild its army.
This cuts across Israel's own vision of the neighborhood.
Aydintasbas calls Israel's strategy in the region after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel that killed almost 1,200 people, "mowing the lawn" — a phrase borrowed from the Israeli military itself. Israel's war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 people, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.
"Settling on a regional policy that calls for keeping their neighbors militarily suppressed, giving Israel freedom of action, and making sure that no power rises in the region enough to present a challenge to Israel," she says.
That means a decentralized and fragmented Syria, the southern part of which Israel now controls and shows no signs of ceding.
"In the past, we didn't see Israel and Turkey competing in terms of regional aspirations, or trying to protect or expand their spheres of influence," says Eldad Ben Aharon, a senior researcher at the Peace Research Institute Frankfurt and expert on Israeli-Turkish relations.
In early August, Israel launched an airstrike targeting a defunct airbase in Abu al-Duhur, in northern Syria, to pre-empt an anticipated deployment there of Turkish forces. Both Turkey and Syria denied any such troop movements, and U.S. officials criticized the strike as an " unnecessary escalation ."
Turkey has had a long-standing, if frosty, relationship with Israel. It was the first Muslim-majority country to recognize Israel in 1949, and in 2023 just before Hamas' Oct. 7 attacks, Erdogan and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu shook hands at the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
It was a stark difference from how Erdogan addressed Israel at this year's General Assembly gathering.
"Before us stands a genocidal mindset that can never get enough of killing," Erdogan said from the U.N. podium last week, prompting the Israeli delegation to walk out.
Israel rejects the charge of genocide.
Israeli politicians have not held back either, using rhetoric fueled in part by campaigning for upcoming national elections. Former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett has called Turkey "the new Iran." In August, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz warned Erdogan "not to mess with us," after military tensions rose between the two countries over Syria.
Ben Aharon says it's not out of the realm of possibility that Israel and Turkey could find themselves in a violent conflict in a few years.
"Israel and Turkey now increasingly view each other through a zero-sum lens" he says.

Andy Burnham has been warned against dropping the triple lock on pensions, with the Unite union boss warning it would be "morally wrong" - remind me, what's the triple lock?
Asked whether the commitment should be reformed to fund the PM's social care plans, Sharon Graham says : "Going to a group of people who are getting around Â£12,500 a year in order to pay for it to take away their security is wrong"
Burnham has not said if he's planning to scrap the commitment, which is in Labour's 2024 manifesto, but speculation is rife ahead of his first conference speech as PM
Earlier, Deputy Labour leader Lucy Powell was repeatedly asked about Burnham's plans - she said the party was "absolutely committed" to the triple lock but wanted a "long-term solution" on social care
Yesterday, Chancellor John Healey used his speech to say "the best thing" young people can be offered "is not a benefit payment - it's a first job with training and a wage"
Edited by Charlotte Hadfield and Angus Thompson, with political correspondent Jack Fenwick at Labour's conference in Liverpool
As Burnham's speech approaches, there has been speculation that in order to fund his plans for social care, he could question the long-term viability of the triple lock policy on the state pension.
The policy , which increases the amount paid in the state pension annually, is expected to add billions to the cost of pensions in future years because of the UK's ageing population.
Speaking to BBC Breakfast this morning, deputy Labour leader Lucy Powell says Labour is "committed to the triple lock" for this Parliamnent, as part of the pledge it made in its 2024 manifesto.
Pressed on whether the triple lock would be included in Labour's next manifesto going into the next general election, Powell says "we don't write manifestos now, we're delivering the last manifesto".
"We are talking about how we can deal with these big challenges that the country faces, and they are going to be paid for. Some people are already paying for social care, acutely and profoundly."
Speaking to Radio 4's Today programme, Powell says the party's social care proposals will be in its next manifesto after a ânational conversationâ around finding a "long-term solution" to social care, following Baroness Caseyâs review.
The prime minister is expected to set out his "vision" for offering access to free social care services to everyone in England.
Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, including assistance at home. But the current social care system isn't free, unlike NHS services.
Burnham told the BBC on Sunday he will put his plans before voters at the next general election, saying it would be a system in which "everyone contributes, everyone is covered". He did not rule out tax rises, acknowledging it may be "difficult or unpopular" with some.
Burnham did say the plans won't come into effect until after the general election, as he wanted to stick to the commitments in Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which included a promise not to increase national insurance, income tax or VAT.
Baroness Louise Casey was asked by Burnham to speed up her commission into adult social care in England, and now it's due to be released by April 2027.
Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the PM was suggesting Labour wanted "more tax rises" to pay for the reforms, adding the Conservatives would not support this.
The triple lock is all about state pensions.
It guarantees that the state pension goes up each year in line with whichever is the highest out of inflation, wage increases or 2.5%.
Introduced in 2010 by the Conservative-Liberal Democrat government, it was designed to ensure the value of the state pension wasn't overtaken by the increase of the cost of living or incomes of workers.
In its 2024 manifesto, Labour pledged to retain the triple lock
for the state pension.
According to the Institute for Fiscal Studies, the state pension costs Â£154bn per year, the largest benefit in the UK. It says spending on the state pension is now Â£16bn higher than it would have been without the triple lock.
Currently, the age to claim a state pension is 66, but gradually rising to 67 in a phased approach.
The state pension is a payment made every four weeks by the government, to people who have reached the qualifying age and have paid enough National Insurance contributions.
The general secretary of the Unite union, Sharon Graham, says taking away the triple lock guarantee for pensions would be "morally wrong".
Speaking to the Radio 4's Today programme, Graham says: "It's important that Labour makes sure that working class people know they are on their side, and this would be a direction of travel that would say the opposite to that."
Instead of "trying to pick the pocket of pensioners", Graham says we need "to move over to the other side of the equation, and look at things like wealth taxes, way before we try to stop something like the triple lock".
"It's wrong, and to be fair to Andy (Burnham) he hasn't said that, we haven't heard that come from Andy, this is a rumour that's been floating around since Sunday," she adds.
Graham has previously commented that scrapping the triple lock would be "electoral suicide".
Andy Burnham is set to deliver his first Labour Party conference speech as prime minister today.
Burnham will promise "bold and honest" leadership, saying he will outline policies and commitments that form a "serious prospectus" for Britain and offer people more control over their lives.
Ahead of his speech, the prime minister is facing speculation that in his efforts to free up funding for his social care plans, he could question the long-term sustainability of the "triple lock" uprating policy for the state pension.
Downing Street would not be drawn on whether a review is being considered, while ministers have been clear that a manifesto commitment to keep the triple lock for the duration of this parliament stands.
The prime minister is also expected to announce a new government body to invest in Britain's electricity grid, with the aim of bringing UK energy costs in line with other nations in Europe within ten years.
We're also expecting to hear from Housing Secretary Angela Rayner just before midday, ahead of the prime minister's address at 14:00, which you can watch live here.
Stick with us as we bring you the latest updates and analysis from the conference floor.
In his first Labour Party conference speech as Chancellor, John Healey said the government plans to bring back hope through a "new age of industrialisation", announcing new funding for shipbuilding and manufacturing.
Also addressing the conference this morning were Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, here's what we heard:
We're pausing our live coverage for now, but you can read more in our full story here.
Dharshini David Deputy economics editor
The Chancellorâs speech leant heavily on the concept of hope, but at its heart was a dose of financial reality.
Whatever the governmentâs spending ambitions,
the indication was  the forthcoming Budget would be about fiscal
discipline, rather than extra cash.
We do, after all, spend more on interest
payments on existing public debt than any government department, apart from
health.
But there remains many questions about how the Chancellor
will realise goals such as faster growth and better employment opportunities.
The extra funds for apprenticeships will, for example, be a welcome boost â but
itâs a relatively small one â and many sectors continue to grapple with higher
costs of employing staff, including tax changes imposed by the previous
Chancellor.
So, there is much yet to be resolved â and while optimism is
crucial for a thriving economy, hope alone wonât do the job.

articles.title_orig: MLB playoff predictions: are the Dodgers heading for an inevitable fall?
articles.title_zh: MLB playoff predictions: are the Dodgers heading for an inevitable fall?
articles.content_orig:
As the postseason starts with the wildcard round, our writers pick the dark horses, likely winners and the high seeds at risk of going out early
The Mariners . The only active MLB team to have never appeared in a World Series came within a single win of ending that hoodoo last October and appeared poised to go one stage further in 2026. Instead, their 76-86 clunker feels like a wasted chance for a lineup featuring Julio Rodríguez, Cal Raleigh and Randy Arozarena. BAG
The Pirates could have brought real verve to the postseason with a healthy Konnor Griffin at shortstop and Paul Skenes on the mound. Sadly the team dug too deep a hole in August and, in usual Pirate fashion, didn’t give themselves a chance. AK
That has to be the Orioles , which means Pete Alonso’s F-David Stearns tour won’t see the bright lights of the postseason. The Mets’ president of baseball operations, one with almost all the money in the world at his disposal, who didn’t offer a contract to Alonso – who hit 43 home runs, arguably the second-best season of his career – is finally off the hook. That is, at least until a would-be 2027 season. Too bad. DL
The American League’s No 2 seed is an 85-win division champion with a plus-11 run differential who FanGraphs suggests was closer to a .500 ball club . The Guardians have the pitching to thrive in close games, but a lineup without a 20-homer batter leaves them little room for error. BAG
The Dodgers are finally going to face the consequences that come with age, variance, and having had to play an extra 31 games over the prior two postseasons. They still have no big weaknesses, but their lineup is old (the average age on their roster is 31, making them the oldest team in MLB) and has occasionally looked the part this year. AK
If you needed a team to squeak out a single run under pressure against great playoff pitching, that’s not the Yankees with Aaron Judge in the lineup. Without him, against some superb Red Sox hurlers, the swing-and-a-miss Bronx Bombers have even less of a chance of putting runs on the board. They could find themselves bronzing in Cancún sooner rather than later. DL
It seems odd to call a team with baseball’s best offense and defense a dark horse, but the Cubs ’ leaky relief pitching makes them one. Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman give Chicago plenty of ways to win games. If the bullpen can keep the ball in the park, they could go far. BAG
The Rays will always have a dark-horse feel, even in a year when they win the AL East. Pitching could be the difference here: whether injured starter Shane McClanahan returns at some point or not, the deadline acquisition of Freddy Peralta from the Mets ensures rotation depth that will serve this club well. AK
How can a team with 98 wins be a dark horse? When they don’t hit for power, get on base less than the Rockies, and their ability to score is a little better than middle of the road. They play in a condom-covered dump in front of some of the leanest crowds in the league. An inspiring, title-like set up? Nope, and the Rays are dark horses because few fans know they even exist. Pragmatic as they come though; they can pitch and Kevin Cash can manage. The AL can’t handle them, and the Dodgers are vulnerable. DL
Tarik Skubal arrives in October as the centerpiece of baseball’s most formidable rotation, with a potential record-setting free agency ahead. Every start will be judged against the imposing price the Dodgers paid to acquire him in their bid for a rare third straight title. BAG
Tampa Bay’s Chandler Simpson is a throwback, a defense, speed and batting average-heavy corner outfielder who’s made a place for himself despite lacking the power that makes most great modern hitters. In a lineup with a lot of thump, Simpson’s slap hitting offers a bit of variety. AK
Sticking to my Rays theme, it’s Junior Caminero . The Dominican gets no recognition, or at least not enough, despite crushing close to 90 home runs in two years, while also hitting for average. He’s making strides every season and he’s only 23. At some point the third baseman is going to be very expensive, so who knows how long he’ll remain on the Gulf. At the moment, he’s the straw that stirs Tampa’s tipple, and now Caminero has the spotlight. DL
The labor talks . The collective bargaining agreement expires on 1 December and MLB’s salary-cap proposal remains at odds with the players’ intractable position. A lockout could freeze the hot-stove market while a prolonged dispute could torpedo the 2027 season entirely. Whatever happens on the field, the most important baseball story after the Fall Classic will unfold across a bargaining table. BAG
The lack of great teams in the American League. The Rays may be a great team, but is anyone else in the Junior Circuit? MLB’s three best teams – the Brewers, Dodgers and Braves – are all in the NL, and I’d probably prefer the Cubs over any team in the AL at the moment, too. The AL has a true “anyone’s ballgame” feel. You could imagine this league producing a truly weird pennant winner. AK
The postseason CBA negotiations may not bring us world peace, but hopefully they will create a new rule that bans teams with .500 records or worse from winning a division, or reaching the playoffs via a wildcard spot. The team with the best above-.500 record not to qualify for the playoffs, regardless of league, will replace that team, and the sub-.500 bums will not be allowed to complain AT ALL. And God forbid the Astros win the 2026 World Series, I will pull whatever is left of my hair out. Who’s with me? DL
The Rays will put the ball in play, run the basepaths aggressively and make the Dodgers earn their outs. But a rotation of Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow gives the Dodgers four starters capable of shutting down the Rays’ contact-heavy lineup, while the incandescent Shohei Ohtani supplies the power capable of turning any close game with one swing of the bat. Milwaukee and Tampa Bay may grade out better analytically, but the smell test clearly favors the Dodgers to become only the third franchise to win three consecutive World Series crowns. BAG
The Brewers will finally get the right October mixture this year. They have the same deep lineup as usual, with no real stars but also no weaknesses. Jacob Misiorowski gives them a rotation trump card that they haven’t had since CC Sabathia’s brief run in Milwaukee after the 2008 trade deadline. And they have the necessary high-leverage relievers (Trevor Megill, Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby) to feel good about any game that’s still competitive after six innings. AK
In many ways the Brewers and Rays are mirror images of each other, especially when it comes to their contract-based approaches to baseball. They are also similar in the way that absolutely nobody except their fans wants to see such a matchup. The Brewers have the overwhelming ace in Misiorowski, but the Rays have more pitching depth. They’re also due to win, with the owners detesting this matchup which proves lower payroll teams can win it all. And at precisely the wrong time. DL

articles.title_orig: OpenAI Reportedly Cancels GPT-6.1 Astra's Release Over Deceptive Behavior
articles.title_zh: OpenAI Reportedly Cancels GPT-6.1 Astra's Release Over Deceptive Behavior
articles.content_orig:
It was supposed to debut in October, but it apparently showed higher levels of deception than previous models.
OpenAI has canceled the release of its new model, GPT-6.1 Astra, according to The Wall Street Journal . It was due for launch in October and was going to debut inside ChatGPT and Codex, but it reportedly showed higher levels of deception than its predecessors during internal testing. Saachi Jain, who leaves OpenAI's safety training, said that GPT-6.1 Astra performed poorly on tests that measure how well it adheres to instructions. It also wasn't honest about telling testers the actions it did and didn't perform in order to achieve its goal.
In addition, the model would take actions to accomplish tasks without asking for permission, such as using external tools and services. Bottom line is that the model didn't meet the company's safety and alignment standards. After the Hugging Face incident came to light, OpenAI had admitted that its models were involved in several other events wherein they had escaped their isolated testing environments to break into third party websites and services.
Just last week, the company told The New York Times that its agents had targeted a Commerce Department and a Securities and Exchange Commission website. It also told the publication that it was investigating a supposed incident involving a website operated by the Department of Education. Before that, and in addition to OpenAI's agents hacking into Hugging Face, its agents also broke into Australia's Medicare public health insurance system, a community-ran packaging service for Ruby programs and a German coding forum . The company revealed, as well, that it found more than 50 instances of its agents posting ChatGPT user-provided images to photo-sharing websites.
OpenAI, along with Anthropic, has been calling for an industry-wide slowdown of frontier AI development. "We do not believe that the AI industry has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer," OpenAI previously wrote in a misalignment report. Florida attorney general James Uthmeier petitioned a state court to prevent OpenAI from training new models without independent oversight. "If Sam Altman meant what he said about slowing down, he can join our ask to the court," he said.
The company will still use the same base model for future generations of GPT-6, even though GPT-6.1 Astra has already been scrapped. It will conduct an investigation to identify the root cause of the problems found in the model, Jain said, and will employ reinforcement learning that rewards the correct behavior.

articles.title_orig: News organizations ask court to bar White House enforcement of access ban
articles.title_zh: News organizations ask court to bar White House enforcement of access ban
articles.content_orig:
A logo on a booth for CNN is seen in the press area at the White House, Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026, in Washington. Rod Lamkey/AP hide caption
Three news outlets that President Donald Trump abruptly banished from White House grounds this month asked a federal court to block the ban until the case is resolved, saying the administration has "persisted in unpredictably and inconsistently implementing its ban" despite a judge's restraining order — including selectively barring CNN from White House pool duties.
"The White House's words and actions leave little doubt that it will immediately reinstitute a complete ban of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO if allowed the opportunity," lawyers for CNN, MS NOW and Politico wrote in a filing late Monday.
"Because the ban is an unlawful assault on the most fundamental First Amendment freedoms and will inflict irreparable harm on Plaintiffs and the public if not restrained, this Court should preliminarily enjoin its enforcement pending the resolution of this case," the filing said.
It was the latest development in the back-and-forth saga of the Trump administration and the news media during the second term of his presidency. It has been a contentious relationship that has raised multiple First Amendment questions, produced sanctions and restrictions on White House and Pentagon reporters and led to several lawsuits that are winding their ways through the federal court system.
A two-week temporary restraining order on Trump's ban of the three organizations, issued by U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly last week, restored the outlets' White House access, but expires Oct. 8. The preliminary injunction requested in Monday's filing would extend the White House access until the case is finally resolved.
In a statement emailed to The Associated Press immediately after the filing, the lead attorney for the three news outlets called the ban "a blatant violation of the First Amendment and due process."
"The president and his administration have continued to make clear that this ban has only one purpose: to punish reporting he doesn't like," said the lawyer, Theodore J. Boutrous Jr.
"That's retaliation and viewpoint discrimination, pure and simple," Boutrous said. "With the district court's temporary restraining order expiring this week, it is critical to ensure that the White House continues to be prevented from implementing this unconstitutional ban on the free press."
The filing came a day after the Trump administration made clear it was not backing down from its contention that the sudden ban, which began Sept. 19, was justified.
"When it comes to the White House, it is the people's house," Attorney General Todd Blanche said on ABC on Sunday, invoking an argument the administration has made since the beginning. "It is a privilege, and not a right, to be there."
Monday's 42-page filing reiterated many of the arguments that the news outlets made in their original lawsuit against Trump and the White House, filed two days after the reporters were banned.
It also added mention of the White House broadcast pool rotation, which has become a battleground in the last few days in the standoff between Trump and the media.
The White House, it said, "has persisted in unpredictably and inconsistently implementing its ban, including by barring CNN from fulfilling its role as designated television network pooler on Sept. 26 — to the detriment of CNN, its fellow pool members and, ultimately, the American public."
When the ban was implemented, CNN was removed from its duties as part of the broadcast pool, which consists of the five main networks: CNN, ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News. In solidarity, the other networks decided to suspend the pool until CNN was allowed back in.
On Friday, CNN was allowed to cover the president with Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the National Archives. But in a new setback Saturday, the White House banned the network from Air Force One, preventing it from covering Trump's trip to a college football game in Tennessee. The rest of the pool declined to provide a replacement, in solidarity with CNN.
Blanche defended that decision, too. "The president has every right to decide who gets to fly on his plane," he said in the Sunday interview. He added that Trump was "sick and tired of certain media outlets just refusing to report accurate news." He added that news coverage he described as "misinformation" amounted to a national security issue.
"That is what is a national security problem, when you have complete misinformation coming out of the White House," he said.
Kelly threw cold water on that argument in his ruling last week granting the temporary restraining order against the White House ban. "The court is skeptical … that defendants' interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation" for removal of access, Kelly wrote.
His ruling did not directly address the TV pool rotation. In the new filing, the plaintiffs describe the important function the pool provides and makes the case that it's an important part of the regular access to the president, and his activities, that the media has traditionally had — and must be restored.
It singles out the Air Force One case. "CNN received no official communication from the White House explaining its exclusion," the filing says. "Because CNN was excluded and no replacement designated, no primary television network pooler accompanied the President on the trip."
For now, networks in the pool have decided to address the ongoing standoff on a case-by-case basis, according to a person familiar with the pool's operation, speaking on condition of anonymity to give details of ongoing discussions.
On Sunday, Fox covered a pool event; on Monday, NBC was covering the president in the Oval Office. CNN is not in the rotation until Thursday. If the network is again barred from a pool event, the networks will decide together, presumably based on the newsworthiness of the situation, whether to provide a replacement or to refrain from coverage as they did previously.
The issues at stake are difficult. On the one hand, the networks want to take a stand on behalf of press freedom and against efforts to intimidate coverage. On the other, media outlets have an obvious purpose of providing news to their audiences.
"There are not a lot of good options," said David A. Schulz, director of the Media Freedom and Information Access Clinic at Yale Law School.
Should the White House continue to bar CNN, Schulz said, networks may choose "to exert their market power and say, 'We're not going to play ball with you.'"
The question, Schulz added, is: "Who's going to back down first?"
The networks "may well feel like they're between a rock and a hard place," noted RonNell Andersen Jones, a law professor at the University of Utah.
"Capitulation might be perceived as abandonment of core components of press freedom," Andersen Jones said. "But the practicalities of lengthy White House news blackouts are also complicated, and refusing to cover major news at the highest levels of government might itself feel like a failure to serve the goals of democracy."
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

articles.title_orig: What we know about the lawsuit and investigation into the alleged gang rape at Cornell University
articles.title_zh: What we know about the lawsuit and investigation into the alleged gang rape at Cornell University
articles.content_orig:
A former Cornell University student filed a lawsuit this month alleging she was drugged and gang raped inside a fraternity house in 2024, and the fresh scrutiny has prompted prosecutors to reopen the investigation .
The 101-page lawsuit details disturbing allegations about what the woman, identified as Jane Doe, says unfolded inside Chi Phi’s frat house the night of October 19, 2024, and how the university and local prosecutors in Ithaca, New York, handled the case. Doe is accusing seven members of the frat of participating in the assault while she was unable to consent.
The Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office said Monday it reopened the case to seek a grand jury review after being “asked by the community to revisit the decision whether to pursue criminal charges against the seven fraternity members.”
County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said no criminal charges were initially filed because Doe had not provided police in 2024 with the same key allegations outlined in the new lawsuit.
Doe’s attorney says the information was promptly given to Cornell authorities, and the report was “not materially different from what is contained in the (2026) complaint.”
The legal dispute, lack of criminal charges and university’s response has prompted fierce backlash and revived concerns about how schools respond to allegations of campus sexual assault.
The complaint names more than a dozen defendants, including the seven fraternity members from 2024, Cornell University, and the Chi Phi fraternity. Allegations include negligence, breach of contract, sexual assault and battery, and violations of New York’s Human Rights Law.
CNN has sought comment from the Cornell University Police Department, the Chi Phi fraternity and others named in the lawsuit.
The complaint says Doe was 20 years old and had been drinking at her sorority house and a bar before she arrived at the Chi Phi house to visit a friend, who was one of the fraternity members, on the night of October 19, 2024.
According to the suit, Doe had already consumed about 10 standard drinks within the past three hours when she arrived at the fraternity house.
The complaint alleges the friend and another fraternity member gave her more alcohol and pressured her into snorting a substance they described as ketamine, and that she was then sexually assaulted while “incapable of consent.”
At roughly 1:42 a.m., one of the men allegedly sent a message to the fraternity’s Snapchat group chat – titled “Chi Phi Actives” – stating there was “free p*ssy” upstairs.
By doing this, the suit alleges, one of the accused “encouraged other … chapter members to join in on the gang rape of plaintiff.”
A photo of a portion of the chat is included in the filing. Multiple fraternity members then entered the room, where the complaint alleges they pressured Doe into taking more ketamine and subjected her to an hours-long assault that continued until approximately 5:45 a.m.
An attorney for one of the accused fraternity brothers denied any wrongdoing by his client.
“Even the district attorney’s office, led by a chief prosecutor with the duty to pursue justice and uphold the rule of law without bias or favor, filed no charges against (him) because what she alleged did not happen,” attorney Jeremy Saland said in a statement to CNN. He said his client “never sexually assaulted or even touched the plaintiff in any way.”
An attorney for a different student gave ABC News a statement acknowledging that student participated in the Snapchat conversation mentioned in the complaint but denying that he engaged in sexual activity.
“I did not participate in any sexual activity or drug use. I was not found responsible by Cornell for any of the accusations involving sexual activity and drug use for which others received serious consequences,” the student said through his attorney. “I thoughtlessly engaged in Snapchat and briefly stopped in the room where misconduct happened but not when it happened.”
CNN is working to determine if the other fraternity brothers have representation.
The district attorney said the initial report Jane Doe made to university police differs significantly from the allegations in the lawsuit.
Nothing in Doe’s original statement indicated she was drugged without consent or had sex against her will, Van Houten said. According to the accuser’s statement, “each time Jane Doe asked to stop the sexual conduct, the sexual conduct stopped.”
Van Houten’s office has not released the full police report. CNN has asked Doe’s attorney for a response to Van Houten’s statement and for a copy of her complete 2024 police statement.
During a contentious interview Monday, CNN’s Jake Tapper pressed Van Houten on why there wasn’t a more expansive investigation from law enforcement or the DA’s office after the initial report was made in 2024.
“We can’t change what happened in the past as much as the community is outraged,” Van Houten said. “My job under the New York State Constitution is to apply the penal law of New York state. We are constrained by that law. Whether you agree with it, whether you think someone’s conduct is morally repugnant or vulgar or disgusting. I’m still constrained by the law.”
Van Houten acknowledged that the text message screen shots between the men “were completely vulgar and disgusting, but they had nothing to do with her consent.”
Tapper asked when Van Houten got copies of the text messages, included in the complaint, that the fraternity brothers sent each other.
Van Houten said that his team did not see the text messages evidence initially.
“They were not part of our initial analysis, but I understand that Cornell had them, and they sent them to our team,” he said.
Earlier, Doe’s attorney, Thomas P. Giuffra said in a statement he believes the initial investigation was inadequate.
“It is challenging for me to understand how a thorough criminal investigation could have been conducted when she never spoke with anyone other than the officer who took her original complaint,” Giuffra said.
“Other than her initial contact with Cornell police, she was not contacted by investigators from the Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office or any investigators trained in interviewing rape survivors,” Giuffra said.
“If the district attorney’s office is now considering prosecution, I believe that it is a step in the right direction, albeit a late one.”
The Ithaca Police Department said Monday that it was “disturbed” to hear about the 2024 allegations. The department noted it learned about the alleged incident only recently through the media and said the incident was not reported to the agency.
Doe reported the incident to Cornell University police on November 8, 2024, the complaint says.
Doe’s attorney said Cornell expelled two of the seven accused students while the others received lesser punishment, including suspensions, workshops or written assignments.
Cornell countered that claim Monday, saying there was a range of sanctions for the accused students, including suspensions and expulsions. But “none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement,” the university said.
In a September 21 statement, Cornell declined to confirm the individual disciplinary outcomes, citing federal student privacy law. The school said violations of university policy “could lead to sanctions up to and including suspension or expulsion,” adding, “We will respond in detail through the legal process.”
The sanctions came after it conducted a formal Title IX investigation, separate from the criminal proceeding, and a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days, the school said.
The school also said it had closed the chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity, and that the chapter remains barred from campus.
The lawsuit faults Cornell for failing to properly discipline after the assault, “all the while sheltering them from speaking to law enforcement, and silencing victims.
